title: How Sugar from Outer Space Became One of the Backbones of Life on Earth - Nautilus
gist: A Scientific Reports study using real borate crusts from the Puga hot springs in the Himalayas finds that ribose — a fragile sugar delivered by meteorites — helps borate minerals dissolve, creating a two-way relationship in which borate protects ribose and ribose keeps boron available, suggesting prebiotic organic molecules shaped mineral formation before life existed.

insights.claim: A new study in Scientific Reports using real minerals, including borate crusts from the Puga hot springs, found that ribose helps borate minerals dissolve and inhibits formation of solid grains, keeping more boron dissolved and available for reactions.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Advances origin-of-life chemistry; no direct market implication.
insights.quote: We found that ribose helps borate minerals dissolve and inhibits the formation of solid grains.

insights.claim: The authors propose a two-way relationship in early Earth chemistry: borate protects ribose from breakdown, while ribose keeps borate dissolved and available.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing chemical loop is a candidate mechanism for how fragile biomolecules could persist before life.
insights.quote: Borate protects ribose from breakdown, while ribose helps keep borate dissolved and available.

insights.claim: Ribose may have helped explain how high concentrations of dissolved boron existed in fluids on Earth before life began, resolving a puzzle since boron minerals normally dissolve poorly.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Shifts origin-of-life models toward organics actively shaping their mineral environment.

insights.claim: RNA is thought to have been important in the origin of life but forms with difficulty because its backbone contains ribose, a fragile sugar that breaks down into brown goop when heated, much as table sugar caramelizes.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Background constraint that any origin-of-life scenario must solve.

insights.claim: Boron in the form of borate binds to ribose and helps prevent it from breaking down.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Mechanistic link that makes boron-rich environments prime candidates for where life began.
insights.locator: One thing that can protect ribose molecules

themes.theme: Puga hot springs as lab realism check

insights.claim: Lab origin-of-life experiments often use purified chemicals that isolate reactions but omit interactions in nature's messy chemistry; the authors aim for realism grounded in ancient rocks, minerals and fossils.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Critique of idealized lab conditions — results from purified setups may not transfer to natural environments.
insights.quote: it can leave out important interactions in nature’s “messy” chemistry
insights.locator: Researchers try to recreate these processes

insights.claim: The Puga hot springs in India's Himalayas are so boron-rich that borate salt crusts crunch underfoot like snow, yet their waters hold only a few percent of the boron concentration used in some purified-ingredient lab experiments.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Shows lab boron levels may be unrealistically high relative to natural analog environments.
insights.quote: borate salt crusts crunch underfoot like snow
insights.locator: The waters at Puga contain so much boron

insights.claim: Boron-containing minerals often dissolve poorly in water and precipitate as crystals, leaving less boron available for prebiotic reactions.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Explains why dissolved-boron availability was an open problem for origin-of-life models.

insights.claim: Around four billion years ago Earth had little atmospheric oxygen, far more volcanism and green iron-rich oceans, and meteorites delivered water and carbon compounds — an estimated million tonnes of carbon per year during early bombardment.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Context for exogenous delivery of life's building blocks.
insights.quote: Researchers estimate around a million tonnes of carbon could have arrived each year during this early bombardment.

insights.claim: The Murchison meteorite, which fell in Victoria in 1969 and smelled of kerosene, has been found to contain ribose alongside other sugars.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that ribose can arrive from space.

insights.claim: Without microbes, carbon-containing molecules could accumulate wherever supply outpaced breakdown, for example through evaporation in shallow lakes concentrating organics from space into rich chemical soups.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Identifies evaporative pools as plausible cradles of prebiotic chemistry.

insights.claim: The authors propose that non-living carbon molecules may have begun influencing mineral formation on Earth before life existed, a prebiotic analog of biomineralisation.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Reframes early geochemistry; relevant to astrobiology and where to search for life elsewhere.
insights.quote: We propose non-living carbon molecules may have begun influencing mineral formation even before life existed on Earth.

insights.claim: Ribose was probably relatively rare, but more abundant molecules such as ethylene glycol and glycerol also bind borate, and silica and calcium interact with carbon molecules, suggesting broader effects of primordial soups on rock formation that still need testing.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Opens a testable research line on organic-mineral interactions.
insights.locator: Ribose itself was probably relatively rare.

insights.claim: Boron that would otherwise have formed buried mineral crusts may instead have stayed dissolved in primordial lakes, potentially changing which minerals formed at Earth's surface; whether such interactions reshaped whole landscapes remains open.
insights.speaker: Martin Van Kranendonk
insights.so_what: Speculative but could inform how to read ancient mineral records for life signals.
